# ADR-0009: Qt confined to the application

> **Status:** accepted | **Date:** 2026-07-29

**References:** [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license), [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host), [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate), [RFC-0006:C-OVERLAY](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-overlay), [RFC-0006:C-RENDER](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-render), [RFC-0006:C-SURFACE](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-surface), [RFC-0006:C-TOOLKIT](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-toolkit)

## Context

The renderer has to draw into something the graphical toolkit controls, and the obvious approaches were
foreclosed by constraints already in force.

Licensing decided the shape before graphics did. Qt's open-source terms are LGPL-3.0 and GPL-3.0, and
[RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 4 forbids any dependency beyond `Apache-2.0 OR MIT` beneath a library crate. Qt
therefore cannot appear beneath the renderer at all; it belongs only in the application, which is
`AGPL-3.0-or-later`. This reframed the question entirely: not how Rust talks to Qt, but what surface the
renderer accepts such that the application can obtain one from Qt.

A loophole in that reasoning needed closing. Qt is also sold commercially, and under a commercial licence
its copyleft obligations do not apply — so it can be argued that a Qt dependency beneath a library crate
is compliant *for this project*. It would not be compliant for anyone else: a crate published as
`Apache-2.0 OR MIT` while requiring Qt silently obliges every adopter to accept LGPL terms or buy a
licence, making the declared licence misleading in precisely the way that clause exists to prevent.

Three further constraints narrowed what the renderer may be. It may not block
([RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 4). Its data requests must be cancellable without draining dispatched work
([RFC-0006:C-RENDER](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-render) 2) — and a renderer that blocks on presentation cannot observe a cancellation. And
it must compile for a host with no threads ([RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) 1), so it cannot own a render
thread. Together these rule out the ordinary embedded-renderer arrangement, which spawns a render thread
and blocks on present.

Among bindings, `cxx-qt` from KDAB is the realistic choice: CXX-based, generates QObject subclasses from
Rust, integrates with Qt's build system, actively maintained. `qmetaobject-rs` is lighter but thinner on
QML and less maintained; hand-written `cxx` bridges mean writing the QObject glue by hand; the older
`ritual`-generated bindings are effectively abandoned. Because the toolkit is confined to the
application, this choice sits outside any published contract and can change without governance.

For compositing wgpu output into a Qt scene, three routes existed. Qt's sanctioned path —
`QRhiWidget` and `QQuickRhiItem`, Qt 6.7 and later — expects *Qt's* RHI rather than wgpu, so sharing a
device means importing external memory per backend: Vulkan external memory extensions, D3D12 shared
handles, Metal surfaces. Rendering to an offscreen wgpu texture and importing it as a Qt scene-graph
texture is smaller in surface area but still needs native handle interop per backend. Giving wgpu a
native window handle from a `QWindow` and letting it own that surface avoids interop entirely, at the
cost that the viewport is not composited into the scene graph, so toolkit content cannot overlay it.

Examining what overlay is actually for settled the sequencing. Depth-dependent content — a measurement
anchored to a point behind a stand — cannot be composited correctly at all, because composited content
carries no depth and floats in front of geometry it should be behind; such content has to be drawn by the
renderer regardless of route. What genuinely wants overlay is depth-insensitive interface chrome, which is
valuable but not urgent.

## Decision

The renderer accepts an opaque native surface handle from its host and presents to it directly; the
application obtains that handle from Qt, and Qt appears nowhere else. Offscreen compositing is admitted
by the same contract and adopted when depth-insensitive overlay is wanted. The obligations are written in
[RFC-0006:C-TOOLKIT](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-toolkit), [RFC-0006:C-SURFACE](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-surface) and [RFC-0006:C-OVERLAY](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-overlay); this ADR records only *why*.

Why the toolkit is **confined to the application**:

- **Licensing forbids the alternative.** Qt's open-source terms are LGPL-3.0 and GPL-3.0, beyond what
  [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 4 permits beneath a library crate.
- **The commercial-licence loophole is closed deliberately.** A commercial Qt licence would remove the
  copyleft obligation for this project while leaving every adopter of an `Apache-2.0 OR MIT` crate
  obliged to accept LGPL or buy a licence. [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 4 states this in general form, because
  the same argument arrives for any dual-licensed dependency.
- **The architectural reason outlives the licensing one.** A renderer that knows its toolkit is adoptable
  only by applications using that toolkit, which defeats the purpose of publishing it permissively.

Why the renderer takes a **surface it does not own**:

- **It cannot own a thread or block.** [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) 1 and [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 3 and 4 rule
  out the ordinary embedded-renderer arrangement. The host drives frames; the renderer is a function from
  state to drawn output. This is also what makes [RFC-0006:C-RENDER](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-render) 2 achievable, since a renderer
  blocked on presentation cannot observe a cancellation.
- **A native handle is universal and free.** Every windowing system exposes one, and so does a browser
  canvas — so this satisfies portability with no second code path.

Why **direct presentation first**, and offscreen compositing second:

- **It defers all graphics interop.** Sharing a device with the toolkit's own renderer needs external
  memory import per backend — Vulkan extensions, D3D12 shared handles, Metal surfaces — which is
  platform-specific work unrelated to point clouds, spent before the out-of-core claim is demonstrated.
- **The urgent half of the overlay benefit does not exist.** Depth-dependent content cannot be
  composited correctly under *any* route, because composited content carries no depth and floats in front
  of geometry it should occlude — a measurement anchored behind a stand would read as belonging to the
  near surface. Such content must be renderer-drawn regardless, which is what
  [RFC-0006:C-OVERLAY](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-overlay) 1 requires. What overlay genuinely enables is depth-insensitive chrome:
  valuable, not urgent.
- **The transition costs nothing later because it is admitted now.** [RFC-0006:C-SURFACE](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-surface) 4 requires
  the renderer to accept a target it does not present, since rendering into a host-composited target is a
  superset of presenting to a surface. Adopting offscreen compositing therefore changes the application,
  not the renderer's published contract.

`cxx-qt` is the intended binding, and is deliberately *not* governed: it lives entirely in the
application, so it is a reversible implementation choice rather than a contract, and a churning binding
in the copyleft application layer is a far smaller risk than one beneath a permissive library.

## Consequences

### Positive

No graphics interop work in the first release, so effort goes to the out-of-core claim instead of per-backend
external memory. The renderer stays toolkit-agnostic and therefore adoptable, which is the point of
publishing it permissively. A browser target needs no second path, since a canvas yields the same kind of
handle. Depth-correct content is straightforward because wgpu is authoritative over the 3D path.

### Negative

Toolkit content cannot overlay the viewport until offscreen compositing is adopted, so the interface is
chrome around a viewport rectangle — a real constraint on layout. Anything drawn inside the viewport,
including text, must be drawn by the renderer. The viewport region also does not participate in toolkit
layering or transforms.

### Neutral

The chrome-around-a-rectangle arrangement is what CloudCompare and QGIS's 3D view both use, so it is
conventional rather than a regression — whether it reads as a limitation depends on the interface being
designed, not on the decision.

Offscreen compositing is planned rather than hypothetical and is admitted by [RFC-0006:C-SURFACE](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-surface) 4, so
the work is an application change when wanted. The binding choice is likewise reversible, being confined to
the application and outside any published contract.

Two drifts to watch. First, depth-dependent content being composited by the toolkit because drawing text
there is far easier than drawing it in the renderer — the result looks correct in any screenshot where
nothing occludes it, which is why [RFC-0006:C-OVERLAY](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-overlay) 1 prohibits it rather than discouraging it. Second,
a toolkit dependency reaching a library crate transitively through a convenience crate, which breaks nothing
visible and no test detects; hence the graph check in [RFC-0006:C-TOOLKIT](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-toolkit) 1.

Reversal cost is low in the intended direction and unavailable in the other. Moving to offscreen compositing
is additive and touches the application only. Reversing the toolkit confinement is not available at all,
since it would breach [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 4.

## Alternatives Considered

### Renderer accepts an opaque native surface handle and presents to it directly; the application obtains the handle from a QWindow (accepted)

- **Pros:** No graphics interop at all — no external memory import, no per-backend handle translation, Keeps the renderer free of any toolkit dependency, as [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 4 requires, A native surface handle is also what a browser canvas exposes, satisfying [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) with no second path, wgpu stays authoritative over the 3D path, so depth-correct content is straightforward, Admitting an offscreen target in the same contract makes the later transition an application change only
- **Cons:** The viewport is not composited into the scene graph, so toolkit content cannot overlay it, Fights toolkit layering and transforms applied to the viewport region, Text and chrome drawn inside the viewport must be drawn by the renderer

### Render to an offscreen wgpu texture and import it as a toolkit scene-graph texture

- **Pros:** Viewport composites into the scene graph, so depth-insensitive chrome can overlay it, wgpu remains authoritative over the 3D path, Smaller interop surface than sharing a device with the toolkit's own renderer
- **Cons:** Still requires native texture handle interop per graphics backend, Platform-specific work in exactly the areas that are hardest to test, An extra copy or import per frame relative to presenting directly

### Use the toolkit's own rendering abstraction as the backend, dropping wgpu (rejected)

- **Pros:** Native compositing with no interop whatsoever; the sanctioned path, Overlay, layering and transforms all work as the toolkit intends
- **Cons:** Puts the toolkit beneath the renderer, which [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 4 forbids outright, Renderer becomes unusable by any tool not built on that toolkit, defeating permissive publication, Forecloses a browser target, since the abstraction does not exist there
- **Rejected because:** It requires the toolkit to be a dependency of a library crate, which licensing prohibits and which would make the renderer adoptable only by applications using the same toolkit. Publishing these crates permissively is intended to make them shared infrastructure; a renderer welded to one toolkit is the opposite.

### Share a graphics device between wgpu and the toolkit's renderer via external memory, using the toolkit's RHI widget classes (rejected)

- **Pros:** The toolkit's officially supported integration path for foreign renderers, Full compositing with the scene graph from the outset
- **Cons:** Requires external memory import per graphics backend — Vulkan extensions, D3D12 shared handles, Metal surfaces, Platform-specific graphics work with nothing to do with point clouds, before the core claim is proven, Device sharing failures are notoriously difficult to diagnose and vary by driver
- **Rejected because:** It spends months on per-backend graphics interop before the out-of-core claim the project exists to prove has been demonstrated. The overlay capability it buys is only needed for depth-insensitive chrome, since depth-dependent content must be renderer-drawn under any route — so the urgent half of the benefit does not exist.
